newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jordan's king to try to patch ties with Israel.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's king to try to patch ties with Israel.

text.p: Jordan's King Hussein visits Israel on Sunday to pay condolences to the families of seven schoolgirls killed by one of his soldiers and to try to defuse tensions with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The king expressed shame and shock after the attack, which came after Jordanian-Israeli relations had deteriorated sharply over Netanyahu's settlement plans in Arab East Jerusalem.
"It is very important for Jordan and Israel to put their crisis behind them," Netanyahu's foreign policy adviser, Dore Gold, told CNN.
But the rift seemed unlikely to be bridged easily, especially since Israel vowed to break ground this week for a new Jewish settlement close to East Jerusalem despite an international outcry.

Jordanian army driver Sergeant Ahmed Mousa Mustafa al-Daqamsa opened fire on Thursday on schoolgirls visiting a strip of Jordanian land south of the Sea of Galilee leased to Israel under a 1994 peace treaty.
King Hussein, accompanied by Netanyahu, was due to meet bereaved families in Bet Shemesh near Jerusalem and visit a hospital to see girls wounded in the attack.

The two leaders were later to hold talks and give a joint news conference. King Hussein last visited Jerusalem for the funeral of his peace partner Yitzhak Rabin, the Israeli leader assassinated in 1995.

The king launched a bitter attack on Netanyahu last week over his decision to build 6,500 Jewish homes at Jabal Abu Ghneim, called Har Homa by Israel. He accused Netanyahu of pushing the region "towards an abyss of bloodshed."

The harsh language marked the deepest crisis in ties between the two states since they signed a peace treaty in 1994. Some Israeli ministers said Arab warnings of violence were a factor in Thursday's shooting.

The king was likely to make a last-minute appeal to Netanyahu to scrap the settlement plan, but Gold said Israel would not be swayed. "We've made clear our differences and Jordan has its strong principles that we understand," he said.

Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat summoned Middle East peace sponsors on Saturday as part of his campaign to halt the project, which would tighten Israel's grip on Jerusalem and weaken the Palestinian position in talks due to start this week on the city's "final status"
Asked how Palestinians would react when Israel sent in the bulldozers to begin construction, Arafat said: "I don't know. Ask the Palestinian masses."
Israeli Police Minister Avigdor Kahalani said Israel was ready for any possible explosion of violence.
"The battle for Jerusalem is not just any battle," he told army radio. "If they (Palestinians) try to escalate the situation, the state of Israel has the tools to respond."
